opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today’s readings seem difficult at first, especially Ezekiel. But when they are read together, they carry one very clear message: God is asking us to look honestly at what we hold onto so tightly that we might choose it over Him.

In Ezekiel 24:15–23, God tells Ezekiel that he is about to lose “the delight of his eyes”—his wife. Even more difficult, Ezekiel is told not to mourn her in the customary public way.

This does not mean that Ezekiel should not love his wife or that God considers grief wrong. Ezekiel’s loss becomes a prophetic sign for the people of Israel. They are about to lose Jerusalem and the Temple, things they believed would always be there. They had placed their security in them while gradually moving away from the God who had given them everything.

Then Deuteronomy explains what has gone wrong:

“You were unmindful of the Rock that begot you; you forgot the God who gave you birth.”

That may be the key to understanding all three readings.

The people had not simply made mistakes. They had allowed other things to take God’s place. Their security, desires, and other gods had become more important than their relationship with Him.

Then we come to Matthew 19:16–22 and the rich young man.

This man seems to be doing everything right. He approaches Jesus because he wants eternal life. He has kept the commandments. Yet he knows something is missing, because he asks Jesus:

“What do I still lack?”

Jesus goes directly to the place where this man’s heart is not free.

He tells him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and then, “Come, follow me.”

The man walks away sad because he has many possessions.

His possessions were not necessarily evil. His problem was that when he had to choose between holding onto them and completely following Jesus, he could not let them go.

That is where these readings become personal.

We can follow commandments. We can pray. We can go to church. We can try to live good lives. And still there may be something within us that we hold onto more tightly than we hold onto God.

It may be money, but it may have nothing to do with money.

It could be a relationship. Security. Control. Success. Our reputation. Our plans for the future. The need to be loved. The need for another person to behave the way we believe they should. It can even be the life we imagined we were supposed to have.

None of these things is automatically wrong.

The question is what happens when we cannot surrender them.

God is not necessarily telling us that He intends to take away everything we love. That would miss the point. Instead, these readings ask us to examine where we have placed our ultimate security.

The rich young man wanted eternal life, but Jesus showed him the one place he was still holding back.

And perhaps that is the question for us today:

What do I still lack?

What is the thing I would have the hardest time placing completely into God’s hands?

What am I afraid would happen if I stopped trying to control it?

What have I begun depending upon for my security, happiness, or identity instead of God?

The deepest message of these readings may not be, “Give everything up.”

It may be something much more personal:

Do not forget the God who gave you everything.

Love the people God has given you. Be grateful for your home, your work, your relationships, and the things that bring you joy. But do not ask any of them to become your God.

Because eventually Jesus’ invitation comes down to something very simple:

Trust Me enough to loosen your grip—and follow Me.
